lec05kp25-u01-p1-title.name: u01-p1-title
lec05kp25-u01-p1-title.text: Can a weak classifier only a little better than guessing be boosted into a strong one?

lec05kp25-u01-p1-bridge.name: u01-p1-bridge
lec05kp25-u01-p1-bridge.text: The combining of KP24 needs members that differ. Can one very weak classifier, retrained each time on the points it got wrong, be combined into a strong one?

lec05kp25-u01-p1-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp25-weak
lec05kp25-u01-p1-fig1.text: Test errors of the 20 stumps 'x_j>0?' range from about 27% to 36%, mean 31.6%; the best stump of round 1 has 25.5% on training and 28.75% on test.

image.alt: Test errors of the 20 stumps 'x_j>0?' range from about 27% to 36%, mean 31.6%; the best stump of round 1 has 25.5% on training and 28.75% on test.

lec05kp25-u01-p1-term:弱分類器.name: term:Weak classifier
lec05kp25-u01-p1-term:弱分類器.text: **Weak classifier**: one whose error is only a little better than guessing (0.5).

lec05kp25-u01-p1-term:決策樁.name: term:Stump
lec05kp25-u01-p1-term:決策樁.text: **Stump**: a tree that asks one question about one feature, such as '$x_j>0$?'.

lec05kp25-u01-p1-c1.name: u01-p1-c1
lec05kp25-u01-p1-c1.text: **Setup** (designed here): two 20-D Gaussians (means $\mp a$, $a=2/\sqrt{20}$), 200 training, 400 test points; the 20 stumps '$x_j>0$?' err 27% to 36%, mean 31.6%.

lec05kp25-u01-p1-c2.name: u01-p1-c2
lec05kp25-u01-p1-c2.text: **Mechanism**: reweight the samples every round, giving hard points more weight, then take a weighted vote.

lec05kp25-u01-p2-title.name: u01-p2-title
lec05kp25-u01-p2-title.text: Minimizing the exponential loss stage by stage, the sample weights emerge by themselves

lec05kp25-u01-p2-bridge.name: u01-p2-bridge
lec05kp25-u01-p2-bridge.text: Every round gives the hardest points more weight. Are the weights designed out of thin air?

lec05kp25-u01-p2-term:逐級最佳化.name: term:Stage-wise optimization
lec05kp25-u01-p2-term:逐級最佳化.text: **Stage-wise optimization**: optimize only the newly added classifier and freeze the earlier ones: $F_m=F_{m-1}+\alpha_m\phi_m$.

lec05kp25-u01-p2-c1.name: u01-p2-c1
lec05kp25-u01-p2-c1.text: **Exponential loss**: $\sum_i\exp(-y_iF(x_i))$ (KP20); split stage by stage it becomes $\sum_iw_i\exp(-y_i\alpha\phi(x_i))$ with $w_i=\exp(-y_iF_{m-1}(x_i))$.

lec05kp25-u01-p2-c2.name: u01-p2-c2
lec05kp25-u01-p2-c2.text: **The weights** contain neither $\alpha$ nor $\phi$, so they are the sample weights; $\phi_m$ then minimizes the weighted error $P_m$ (weights normalized to sum 1).

lec05kp25-u01-p3-title.name: u01-p3-title
lec05kp25-u01-p3-title.text: α = ½ln((1−P)/P): a large voice as P→0, zero at P=0.5, negative for P>0.5

lec05kp25-u01-p3-bridge.name: u01-p3-bridge
lec05kp25-u01-p3-bridge.text: The sample weights emerge and $\phi_m$ minimizes the weighted error $P_m$. How much say $\alpha_m$ should it have in the final vote?

lec05kp25-u01-p3-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp25-alpha
lec05kp25-u01-p3-fig1.text: α=½ln((1−P)/P) against the weighted error P: 1.099 at P=0.1, 0.424 at 0.3, 0 at 0.5 and −0.424 at 0.7.

image.alt: α=½ln((1−P)/P) against the weighted error P: 1.099 at P=0.1, 0.424 at 0.3, 0 at 0.5 and −0.424 at 0.7.

lec05kp25-u01-p3-c1.name: u01-p3-c1
lec05kp25-u01-p3-c1.text: **Derivation**: back in $J$, $\alpha_m=\arg\min\{e^{-\alpha}(1-P_m)+e^{\alpha}P_m\}$ and a zero derivative gives $\alpha_m=\tfrac12\ln\tfrac{1-P_m}{P_m}$.

lec05kp25-u01-p3-c3.name: u01-p3-c3
lec05kp25-u01-p3-c3.text: **Meaning**: accurate → a large voice; guessing → 0; worse than guessing ($P>0.5$) → negative, use its answer inverted.

lec05kp25-u01-p4-title.name: u01-p4-title
lec05kp25-u01-p4-title.text: The weight update: wrong points are multiplied by e^α, right ones by e^−α, and the 3 wrong points then hold 0.5

lec05kp25-u01-p4-bridge.name: u01-p4-bridge
lec05kp25-u01-p4-bridge.text: An accurate classifier gets a large voice, guessing gets 0 and worse than guessing a negative one. The same $\alpha$ also sets how far the weights move: work through 10 points with 3 wrong.

lec05kp25-u01-p4-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp25-update
lec05kp25-u01-p4-fig1.text: Ten points of weight 0.1 with 3 wrong, P=0.3 and α=0.4236: after the update the wrong ones have 0.1667 each and the right ones 0.0714 each, so the 3 wrong points hold 0.5.

image.alt: Ten points of weight 0.1 with 3 wrong, P=0.3 and α=0.4236: after the update the wrong ones have 0.1667 each and the right ones 0.0714 each, so the 3 wrong points hold 0.5.

lec05kp25-u01-p4-c1.name: u01-p4-c1
lec05kp25-u01-p4-c1.text: **Update**: $w_i\leftarrow w_i\exp(-y_i\alpha_m\phi_m(x_i))/Z_m$; wrong points ($y\phi<0$) grow and right ones shrink.

lec05kp25-u01-p4-c2.name: u01-p4-c2
lec05kp25-u01-p4-c2.text: **By hand** (designed here): 10 points of weight 0.1, 3 wrong: $P=0.3$, $\alpha=0.4236$; wrong ones times $e^{\alpha}=1.5275$ (0.1528), right ones times $e^{-\alpha}=0.6547$ (0.0655); $Z=0.9165$.

lec05kp25-u01-p4-c3.name: u01-p4-c3
lec05kp25-u01-p4-c3.text: **Normalized**: wrong ones 0.1667 each, right ones 0.0714 each; the three wrong points together hold exactly 0.5 and the next $\phi$ must look after them first.

lec05kp25-u01-p5-title.name: u01-p5-title
lec05kp25-u01-p5-title.text: AdaBoost in a few lines; Example 4.3 redone with 20-D Gaussians and stumps

lec05kp25-u01-p5-bridge.name: u01-p5-bridge
lec05kp25-u01-p5-bridge.text: The weights and the voice are both in place. Strung into an algorithm and run on a real example, what happens?

lec05kp25-u01-p5-c1.name: u01-p5-c1
lec05kp25-u01-p5-c1.text: **Algorithm**: $w_i=1/N$; repeat: find $\phi_m$ minimizing $P_m$, compute $\alpha_m$, update and normalize the weights; finally $f(x)=\operatorname{sign}\sum_k\alpha_k\phi_k(x)$.

lec05kp25-u01-p5-c2.name: u01-p5-c2
lec05kp25-u01-p5-c2.text: **Setup** (Example 4.3 redone here): two 20-D Gaussians, 200 training and 400 test points; each round picks the best stump over all features and thresholds; 2000 rounds.

lec05kp25-u01-p5-c3.name: u01-p5-c3
lec05kp25-u01-p5-c3.text: **Round 1**: training error 25.5% and test error 28.75%, better than an arbitrary fixed stump (mean 31.6%).

lec05kp25-u01-p6-title.name: u01-p6-title
lec05kp25-u01-p6-title.text: Training error hits 0 at round 17 and the test error falls to 3.25% near round 200, then stays near 4%

lec05kp25-u01-p6-bridge.name: u01-p6-bridge
lec05kp25-u01-p6-bridge.text: Round 1 gave training error 25.5% and test error 28.75%. Should one keep running after the training error hits zero, and where does the test error go?

lec05kp25-u01-p6-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp25-curve
lec05kp25-u01-p6-fig1.text: Training and test error against rounds (log axis): training error is 0 from round 17 and the test error falls from 28.75% to 3.25% at round 200, then stays near 4%.

image.alt: Training and test error against rounds (log axis): training error is 0 from round 17 and the test error falls from 28.75% to 3.25% at round 200, then stays near 4%.

lec05kp25-u01-p6-c1.name: u01-p6-c1
lec05kp25-u01-p6-c1.text: **Training error**: 25.5% at round 1, 4.5% at round 10 and 0 from round 17 on.

lec05kp25-u01-p6-c3.name: u01-p6-c3
lec05kp25-u01-p6-c3.text: **Meaning**: after the training error reaches zero the test error keeps falling, then stays near 4% after about 200 rounds, flat within sampling error (with 400 test points 1% is only 4 points).

lec05kp25-u01-p7-title.name: u01-p7-title
lec05kp25-u01-p7-title.text: A common explanation: the margins are pushed up and the bound ignores the number of rounds

lec05kp25-u01-p7-bridge.name: u01-p7-bridge
lec05kp25-u01-p7-bridge.text: The test error did not rise after the training error hit zero. How does the book explain this immunity?

lec05kp25-u01-p7-term:正規化邊距.name: term:Normalized margin
lec05kp25-u01-p7-term:正規化邊距.text: **Normalized margin** $\operatorname{margin}=yF(x)/\sum_k\alpha_k\in[-1,1]$: positive only if correct, larger means more confidence.

lec05kp25-u01-p7-c1.name: u01-p7-c1
lec05kp25-u01-p7-c1.text: **Bound** (Schapire et al.): generalization error $\lesssim\operatorname{prob}\{\operatorname{margin}<\gamma\}+O(\sqrt{V_c/(N\gamma^2)})$, independent of the number of rounds $K$.

lec05kp25-u01-p7-c2.name: u01-p7-c2
lec05kp25-u01-p7-c2.text: **Experiment** (designed here), smallest margin: $-1.000$ at round 1, $-0.205$ at 10, $+0.148$ at 50, $+0.203$ at 200, $+0.220$ at 2000; share with margin $<0.1$: 25.5%, 8.5%, 0%. The bound is loose, a qualitative explanation only.

lec05kp25-u01-p8-title.name: u01-p8-title
lec05kp25-u01-p8-title.text: No panacea: with 15% flipped labels the test error is lowest at 17.8% and then rises to 23.3%

lec05kp25-u01-p8-bridge.name: u01-p8-bridge
lec05kp25-u01-p8-bridge.text: The margins are pushed up all the way. If some training labels are wrong to begin with, is AdaBoost still immune?

lec05kp25-u01-p8-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp25-noise
lec05kp25-u01-p8-fig1.text: Test error against rounds: it falls to 5.5% with clean labels but with 15% flipped labels it is lowest at 17.8% around round 30 and then rises to 23.3%.

image.alt: Test error against rounds: it falls to 5.5% with clean labels but with 15% flipped labels it is lowest at 17.8% around round 30 and then rises to 23.3%.

lec05kp25-u01-p8-c1.name: u01-p8-c1
lec05kp25-u01-p8-c1.text: **Setup** (designed here): data of the same kind with 15% of the training labels flipped; means of 5 fresh draws (unlike the single run before; test labels clean).

lec05kp25-u01-p8-c3.name: u01-p8-c3
lec05kp25-u01-p8-c3.text: **Likely cause**: the exponential loss punishes bad samples with large negative margins too much; after 2000 rounds the 15.5% flipped samples hold 36% of the weight (one run).

lec05kp25-u01-p9-title.name: u01-p9-title
lec05kp25-u01-p9-title.text: Extension: a classifier with P=0.7 has α=−0.424 and its answer is used inverted

lec05kp25-u01-p9-bridge.name: u01-p9-bridge
lec05kp25-u01-p9-bridge.text: The exponential loss concentrates the weights on hard points. If in some round the weighted error is $P_m>0.5$, what happens to $\alpha_m$ and the weight update?

lec05kp25-u01-p9-c2.name: u01-p9-c2
lec05kp25-u01-p9-c2.text: **Used inverted**: $-0.4236\,\phi=+0.4236\,(-\phi)$; the weighted error of $-\phi$ is 0.3.

lec05kp25-u01-p9-c3.name: u01-p9-c3
lec05kp25-u01-p9-c3.text: **Update**: points $\phi$ gets wrong are multiplied by $e^{-0.4236}=0.6547$ (shrink) and points it gets right by 1.5275 (grow), exactly as for the inverted classifier.

lec05kp25-u01-p10-title.name: u01-p10-title
lec05kp25-u01-p10-title.text: Extension: practice, α and the new weights after one round of AdaBoost

lec05kp25-u01-p10-bridge.name: u01-p10-bridge
lec05kp25-u01-p10-bridge.text: A negative $\alpha$ means the answer is used inverted. Back to the plainest round: 5 points with 1 wrong, what are $\alpha$ and the new weights?

lec05kp25-u01-p10-q1.name: u01-p10-q1
lec05kp25-u01-p10-q1.text: **Setup**: 5 samples with weights 0.2 each, 1 misclassified by $\phi$, weighted error $P=0.2$.

lec05kp25-u01-p10-q3.name: u01-p10-q3
lec05kp25-u01-p10-q3.text: **Question 2**: after the update and normalization, what is the weight of each sample?

lec05kp25-u01-p11-title.name: u01-p11-title
lec05kp25-u01-p11-title.text: Extension: worked solution of questions 1 and 2, α=0.6931 and the wrong point holds 0.5

lec05kp25-u01-p11-bridge.name: u01-p11-bridge
lec05kp25-u01-p11-bridge.text: The practice asked for $\alpha$ and the new weights with 1 of 5 points wrong. Worked out in full, what are the answers?

lec05kp25-u01-p11-a2.name: u01-p11-a2
lec05kp25-u01-p11-a2.text: **Question 2**: the wrong one $0.2\times2=0.4$ and each of the 4 right ones $0.2\times0.5=0.1$; $Z=0.4+0.4=0.8$; normalized: 0.5 for the wrong one and 0.125 for each right one.

lec05kp25-u01-p11-a3.name: u01-p11-a3
lec05kp25-u01-p11-a3.text: **Check**: the total is $0.5+4\times0.125=1$; the wrong point holds exactly half, the same pattern as the 3 points holding 0.5 on page 4.

steps.label: Boosting and AdaBoost
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Main line 8 pages plus 3 extension pages (not timed). Self-study deck, English version. Made under CLARITY.md C12 to C18. Whether weak learning can be boosted, the exponential loss and stage-wise optimization, the weights emerging from the exponential loss, the formula and three regimes of alpha, the weight update, the algorithm, the margin explanation of the immunity and the criticism that the bound is loose, the fact that boosting is no panacea and the 'to remember' line follow the source; every number (stump test errors of 27% to 36%, the alpha table, the 10-point hand run, training error reaching 0 at round 17, the margin table, the 15% label-flip experiment, the practice 0.6931, 0.5 and 0.125) was recomputed by a program and these experiments were designed for this lecture (added). The lecture redoes the setup of Example 4.3 (20-D Gaussians, stumps) and states honestly that the test error falls to 3.25% around round 200 and then stays near 4%, that small single-run fluctuations should not be over-read, and that with 15% flipped labels the test error is lowest at 17.8% around round 30 and then rises to 23.3%. Speaker notes are published with the file and contain no student numbers, grades or exam items.

steps.label: Weak to strong
steps.speakerNotes: The combining of KP24 needs members that differ. This page asks whether one very weak classifier, retrained each time on the points it got wrong, can be combined into a strong one. First the weak classifier: one whose error is only a little better than guessing. The stump: a tree that asks one question about one feature, such as whether x_j is above 0. The setup was designed here: two 20-D Gaussians with means minus and plus a, a equal to 2 over root 20, 200 training and 400 test points; the 20 stumps have test errors of 27% to 36%, mean 31.6%. The mechanism: change the sample weights every round, giving the hardest, misclassified points more weight, and take a weighted vote at the end. The next page asks whether the weights are designed out of thin air.

steps.label: Where weights come from
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said every round gives the hardest points more weight. This page asks whether the weights are designed out of thin air. First stage-wise optimization: optimize only the newly added classifier and freeze the earlier ones, F_m being F_{m-1} plus alpha_m times phi_m. The exponential loss, seen in KP20: the sum over samples of exp of minus y times F; split stage by stage it becomes the sum of w_i times exp of minus y alpha phi, with w_i equal to exp of minus y_i F_{m-1}. The weights contain neither alpha nor phi, so they are the sample weights; phi_m then minimizes the weighted error P_m, with the weights normalized to sum 1. The next page asks how much say this classifier should have in the final vote.

steps.label: The voice α
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said phi_m minimizes the weighted error P_m. This page asks how much say alpha_m it should have in the final vote. Derivation: back in the cost, alpha_m minimizes e to the minus alpha times 1 minus P_m plus e to the alpha times P_m, and a zero derivative gives alpha_m equal to a half times the log of 1 minus P_m over P_m. Values: P of 0.1 gives 1.099; 0.3 gives 0.424; 0.5 gives 0; 0.7 gives minus 0.424. The meaning: an accurate classifier has a large voice; guessing has 0; one worse than guessing, with P above 0.5, is negative and its answer is used inverted. The next page looks at how the weights are updated.

steps.label: The weight update
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said a large alpha means a large voice. This page asks how far the same alpha moves the weights, working through 10 points with 3 wrong. The update: w_i times exp of minus y alpha phi, divided by Z_m; wrong points grow and right ones shrink. The hand run was designed here: 10 points of weight 0.1, 3 wrong: P is 0.3 and alpha is 0.4236; wrong ones are multiplied by e to the alpha, 1.5275, giving 0.1528; right ones by e to the minus alpha, 0.6547, giving 0.0655; Z is 0.9165. Normalized: wrong ones 0.1667 each, right ones 0.0714 each; the three wrong points together hold exactly 0.5 and the next phi must look after them first. The next page strings these into the algorithm.

steps.label: The algorithm
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page put the weights and the voice in place. This page asks what happens when they are strung into an algorithm and run on a real example. The algorithm: w_i equal to 1 over N; repeat: find phi_m minimizing P_m, compute alpha_m, update and normalize the weights; finally f of x is the sign of the sum of alpha_k times phi_k. The setup redoes Example 4.3 here: two 20-D Gaussians, 200 training and 400 test points; each round picks the best stump over all features and thresholds; 2000 rounds. Round 1: training error 25.5% and test error 28.75%, better than an arbitrary fixed stump, mean 31.6%. The next page follows the training and test errors.

steps.label: The error curves
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page gave a round-1 training error of 25.5% and a test error of 28.75%. This page asks whether to keep running after the training error hits zero and where the test error goes. Training error: 25.5% at round 1, 4.5% at round 10 and 0 from round 17 on. Test error: 28.75% at round 1; 12.25% at 10; 4.75% at 50; 3.25% at 200; 4.0% at 500; 4.25% at 2000. The meaning is that after the training error reaches zero the test error keeps falling, then stays near 4% after about 200 rounds without rising; small single-run fluctuations, 3.25% against 4.25%, should not be over-read. The next page asks how the book explains this immunity.

steps.label: The margin explanation
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the test error did not rise after the training error hit zero. This page asks how the book explains this immunity. First the normalized margin: y times F of x over the sum of the alphas, in minus 1 to 1, positive only if correct, larger meaning more confidence. The bound, by Schapire and others: the generalization error is roughly at most the probability that the margin is below gamma plus a term depending on V_c over N gamma squared, independent of the number of rounds K. The experiment was designed here, smallest margin: minus 1.000 at round 1, minus 0.205 at 10, plus 0.148 at 50, plus 0.203 at 200, plus 0.220 at 2000; the share with margin below 0.1 is 25.5%, 8.5% and 0%. The criticism: the bound is very loose unless N is in the tens of thousands, so it is only a qualitative explanation; stage-wise optimization is itself an implicit regularization. The next page asks what happens when some labels are wrong to begin with.

steps.label: No panacea
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the margins are pushed up all the way. This page asks whether AdaBoost is still immune if some training labels are wrong to begin with. The setup was designed here: data of the same kind with 15% of the training labels flipped; means of 5 fresh draws (unlike the single run before; test labels clean). Results, test error: clean: 14.4% at 10 rounds, 6.6% at 100 and 5.5% at 2000; 15% flipped: 19.1%, 18.9% and 23.3%, lowest 17.8% at 30 rounds. Why: the exponential loss punishes bad samples with large negative margins too much; after 2000 rounds the 15.5% flipped samples hold 36% of the weight, in one run. This agrees with the book: on hard tasks with a high Bayes error AdaBoost can degrade sharply. The next extension page looks at a negative alpha.

steps.label: Extension: negative α
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the exponential loss concentrates the weights on hard points. This extension asks what happens to alpha_m and the weight update if in some round the weighted error P_m is above 0.5. Alpha: for P equal to 0.7, half times the log of 0.3 over 0.7, which is minus 0.4236. Used inverted: minus 0.4236 times phi equals plus 0.4236 times minus phi; the weighted error of minus phi is 0.3. Update: points phi gets wrong are multiplied by e to the minus 0.4236, which is 0.6547, and shrink; points it gets right are multiplied by 1.5275 and grow, exactly as for the inverted classifier. The next page poses an exercise.

steps.label: Extension: practice
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said a negative alpha inverts the answer. This page poses an exercise back on the plainest round: 5 samples with weights 0.2 each, 1 misclassified by phi, weighted error P equal to 0.2. Question 1: what is alpha? Question 2: after the update and normalization, what is the weight of each sample? Work it out first, then see the next page.

steps.label: Extension: solution
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page posed the exercise and this page is the complete solution. Question 1: alpha is half the log of 0.8 over 0.2, which is half the log of 4, which is 0.6931; e to the alpha is 2 and e to the minus alpha is 0.5. Question 2: the wrong one is 0.2 times 2, which is 0.4, and each of the 4 right ones is 0.2 times 0.5, which is 0.1; Z is 0.4 plus 0.4, which is 0.8; normalized: 0.5 for the wrong one and 0.125 for each right one. Check: the total is 0.5 plus 4 times 0.125, which is 1; the wrong point holds exactly half, the same pattern as the 3 points holding 0.5 on page 4. That finishes boosting and AdaBoost; the next knowledge point looks at class imbalance.

metadata.title: Pattern Recognition, Chapter 4, KP25: boosting and AdaBoost, turning weak into strong (undergraduate, self-study)
